newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Daughters ask UN chief what he does for a living.
newsitem.headline: Daughters ask UN chief what he does for a living.

text.p: Saying he had "never seen this place jumping as it is this morning," Secretary-General Kofi Annan welcomed 600 girls, telling them to make themselves at home and "have a ball."

The daughters of U.N. employees, diplomats and journalists, from 9 to 15 years of age, flocked to the United Nations for "Take our Daughters to Work Day," undergoing tours, lectures, press conferences and chats with women officials and journalists based at the world body.
Annan welcomed them, answering questions such as "How can I become secretary-general?", "What is it you really do?" and "Are you nervous giving speeches?".

"When you become secretary-general ... good luck," he told one questioner and then verbally took the group through a day of meetings, explaining how the rebels would not allow food aid to reach refugees in Zaire.
But he had a prepared message also, saying millions of girls and women around the world had no power and no vote and made up the majority of the world's impoverished.

"Let us be their special voice today," he said. "I encourage you always to keep your minds and eyes open to new ideas, new interests, because as women of the 21st century there will be no limits to what you can accomplish."
Zorah Tabatabai, who organised the event at the United Nations, said she had resisted pressure to invite boys also.
"The parents of daughters and sons, they know why we are doing this, they know the problem of self-esteem for girls. But some of those with only boys or no children disagree with a daughters' day."

Anais Rez, 13, of France, who attends the Lycee Francais in New York, said, "This is an event that should change some views that sexist men have on women and show them that we are being recognised equally."

But 6-year-old Anna Menon, daughter of Indian journalist Bhaskar Menon, had other ideas and used the day for the second consecutive year to sell candy in order to raise funds for her Little League baseball team in Teaneck, New Jersey.
The fifth annual feminist event encouraged workers to bring their daughters or other girls to see the world of work.
